mainEntity.name: How long should a dental crown feel high after fitting?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is common for a crown to feel slightly high or unusual for the first few days after placement, particularly once the anaesthetic wears off. Most patients find that minor discomfort resolves within one to two weeks as the bite settles and surrounding tissues recover. If the crown continues to feel noticeably high, or if discomfort persists beyond two weeks, a follow-up appointment for bite adjustment is recommended. Your dental team can assess the contact points and make any necessary refinements.

mainEntity.name: Why does my crown still feel high after the dentist adjusted it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Even after adjustment, a crown may continue to feel high for several reasons. If the adjustment was made whilst anaesthetic was still active, you may not have been able to feel subtle bite differences accurately. Muscle memory, jaw posture, and gum tissue sensitivity all influence bite perception. Additionally, it can take a short period of time for the jaw muscles to adapt to the new occlusal contact. If the crown continues to feel uncomfortable after a few days, contact your dental practice for a further review.

mainEntity.name: Can a high crown cause jaw pain or headaches?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a crown that is too high can place uneven pressure on the jaw muscles and joints, potentially contributing to jaw tenderness, facial muscle ache, or tension-type headaches. This occurs because the muscles of the jaw work harder to compensate for the altered bite position. These symptoms are not unusual and typically resolve once the crown height is correctly adjusted. If you are experiencing significant jaw discomfort alongside crown-related symptoms, mention this during your dental review appointment.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to need more than one bite adjustment after a crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is common to require more than one adjustment. Crown fitting involves assessing very fine contact points, and multiple refinements are sometimes needed to achieve a comfortable and balanced bite. This is particularly common with molar crowns, which experience greater biting forces, or in patients who have underlying bite imbalances. Each adjustment involves removing only a very small amount of material, and your crown's integrity is not compromised by this process.

mainEntity.name: Could the discomfort mean there is a problem with my tooth's nerve?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, discomfort following crown placement may relate to the underlying tooth's nerve rather than crown height alone. This is more likely if you experience spontaneous pain — aching that occurs without biting or temperature change — or significant sensitivity to hot and cold that does not settle after two weeks. These symptoms do not automatically indicate a serious problem, but they do warrant assessment. Your dentist can evaluate the tooth and advise on whether further investigation is appropriate.

mainEntity.name: What can I do at home if my crown feels too high?

acceptedAnswer.text: At home, you can try to avoid chewing hard or crunchy foods on the side of the crown, and take over-the-counter pain relief in line with the manufacturer's guidance if discomfort is mild. Rinsing gently with warm saltwater may help soothe any surrounding gum sensitivity. However, home measures are not a substitute for professional adjustment. If your crown feels persistently high or uncomfortable, contact your dental practice to arrange a review. Early assessment is always preferable to waiting when dental discomfort persists.
